content.text:
Review target: `https://github.com/william-coronado/syncd/pull/7`

`high effort → 8 inline angles → dedup (no verify) → ≤10 findings`

You are reviewing for **recall** at high effort: catch every real bug a careful
reviewer would catch in one sitting. At this level, catching real bugs matters
more than avoiding false positives. Err on the side of surfacing.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Find candidates (3 correctness angles + 3 cleanup angles + 1 altitude angle + 1 conventions angle, up to 6 each)

Run **8 independent finder angles** in sequence yourself, in THIS context — do NOT spawn subagents for them. Each
surfaces **up to 6 candidate findings** with `file`, `line`, a one-line
`summary`, and a concrete `failure_scenario`.

### Angle A — line-by-line diff scan

Read every hunk in the diff, line by line. Then Read the enclosing function for
each hunk — bugs in unchanged lines of a touched function are in scope (the PR
re-exposes or fails to fix them). For every line ask: what input, state, timing,
or platform makes this line wrong? Look for inverted/wrong conditions,
off-by-one, null/undefined deref, missing `await`, falsy-zero checks,
wrong-variable copy-paste, error swallowed in catch, unescaped regex metachars.

### Angle B — removed-behavior auditor

For every line the diff DELETES or replaces, name the invariant or behavior it
enforced, then search the new code for where that invariant is re-established.
If you can't find it, that's a candidate: a removed guard, a dropped error
path, a narrowed validation, a deleted test that was covering a real case.

### Angle C — cross-file tracer

For each function the diff changes, find its callers (Grep for the symbol) and
check whether the change breaks any call site: a new precondition, a changed
return shape, a new exception, a timing/ordering dependency. Also check callees:
does a parallel change in the same PR make a call unsafe?

### Reuse

The angles above hunt for bugs; this one and the next two hunt for cleanup in
the changed code. Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change fixes the root cause at the right depth rather than
patching a symptom with a fragile bandaid. Special cases layered on shared
infrastructure are a sign the fix isn't deep enough — prefer the simpler, more
general change to the underlying mechanism over adding special cases, and name
that change.

### Conventions (CLAUDE.md)

Find the CLAUDE.md files that govern the changed code: the user-level
~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, the repo-root CLAUDE.md, plus any CLAUDE.md or
CLAUDE.local.md in a directory that is an ancestor of a changed file (a
directory's CLAUDE.md only applies to files at or below it). Read each one
that exists, then check the diff for clear violations of the rules they state.

Only flag a violation when you can quote the exact rule and the exact line
that breaks it — no style preferences, no vague "spirit of the doc"
inferences. In the finding, name the CLAUDE.md path and quote the rule so the
report can cite it. If no CLAUDE.md applies, return nothing for this angle.

Cleanup, altitude, and conventions candidates use the same
`file`/`line`/`summary` shape; in `failure_scenario`, state the concrete
cost (what is duplicated, wasted, harder to maintain, or which CLAUDE.md rule
is broken) instead of a crash. Correctness bugs always outrank cleanup,
altitude, and conventions findings when the output cap forces a cut.

Pass every candidate with a nameable failure scenario through — finders that
silently drop half-believed candidates are the dominant cause of misses.

## Phase 2 — Dedup only (no verify)

Pool all candidates. Dedup near-duplicates only (same defect, same location, same reason → keep one). Do NOT run verifiers; do NOT re-judge. Sort by severity.

## Output

Target **at least 5 findings**. If fewer genuine findings exist, emit what you have — do not invent to hit the floor.

Call the ReportFindings tool once to report this review's results
with `{level, findings}`. `findings` is at most 10 entries ranked
most-severe first; each entry has `file`, `line`, `summary`,
`short_summary` — the claim compressed to ≤60 characters, no rationale
or consequence clause — `failure_scenario`, and `category` — a short kebab-case slug for the angle
that produced it (`correctness`, `simplification`, `efficiency`,
`reuse`, `altitude`, `conventions`, or a more specific slug like
`test-coverage` when one fits better) — plus `verdict` when a verify pass
produced one. If more than 10 survive, keep the 10 most severe. If
nothing survives, call it with an empty array. Do not also print
the findings as text, and do not create or publish an artifact of the review -
the tool call is the report.


## If findings are fixed later

Whenever reported findings get fixed later in this session - the user asks you
to fix them, or later work fixes them incidentally - you MUST call ReportFindings again with the same findings, each
carrying an `outcome`: `fixed`, `no_change_needed` (the finding was wrong or
already handled), or `skipped` (real but not applied). Do not repeat the
findings as text.
Make that call immediately after the fixes land, before any prose summary; the
host UI's per-finding status updates only from it, and without it the findings
stay marked unresolved.

findings.short_summary: Case-only rename permanently wedges sync
findings.summary: CheckCaseAliases folds manifest/baseline paths together with both scans, so a case-only rename (or deleting `Foo` and creating `foo`) is refused before planning, and because the manifest is never updated the refusal repeats forever.
findings.failure_scenario: User renames `Report.pdf` → `report.pdf` locally. Manifest holds `Report.pdf`, local scan has `report.pdf`, remote still has `Report.pdf` → `case-insensitive path collision` on every scoped cycle, remote poll and deep scan. Renaming the remote too doesn't help (manifest still has the old spelling); the only escape is reverting the rename or deleting the manifest DB. Same for fast two-way via `prev` baseline (sync_once.go:359).

findings.short_summary: Holding dirs abort other clients' scans
findings.summary: Transient `.syncd-hold-*` directories are created inside the synced tree (including on the shared remote), and the scanner hard-fails on them before the ignore matcher runs, so any concurrent scan by another machine — or any leftover from a failed post-publish check — aborts the whole cycle.
findings.failure_scenario: Machine A overwrites/deletes a file on the NAS (claimEntry makes `.syncd-hold-…` in that remote dir). Machine B's remote poll walks the share at that moment → `unfinished sync operation` → whole RunRobustOnce fails. Separately, if `check(claimed, leaf)` after publish fails (e.g. a transient SMB read error while hashing), the holding dir is left behind and every cycle on every client errors until someone cleans it up by hand. claim.go's comment says the name is 'excluded from reconciliation', but it isn't.

findings.short_summary: Overwrites/deletes need RENAME_EXCL or hard links
findings.summary: Every robust overwrite, every delete (including network deletes that used to be a plain unlink), and every exclusive publish now requires the destination FS to support RENAME_EXCL/RENAME_NOREPLACE or hard links; on mounts with neither, all such operations fail.
findings.failure_scenario: On a macOS smbfs mount where renameatx_np(RENAME_EXCL) returns ENOTSUP/EINVAL and linkat isn't supported (SMB without unix extensions), checkExclusivePublish fails → RemoveFrom/CopyChecked return 'filesystem cannot safely restore', and absent-dest uploads fail in publishExclusive. Remote deletes, overwrites and new uploads to the NAS all stop. Needs verification against the real Synology mount.

findings.short_summary: mtime now set before fsync/close
findings.summary: The preserved mtime is applied before `tmp.Sync()`/`tmp.Close()`, whereas the old code deliberately set it after closing; on network filesystems, cached writes flushed at fsync/close can bump the mtime to 'now'.
findings.failure_scenario: Download/upload to smbfs or NFS: the write is buffered, UtimesNanoAt sets the source mtime, then Sync flushes data and the server updates last-write time. Destination mtime ≠ source mtime, so the fast reconciler (size+mtime) re-copies forever, and robust HashIfChanged re-hashes every cycle.

findings.short_summary: Scoped cycle loads full manifest names per batch
findings.summary: RunRobustScoped now calls `Repo.LoadNames` (a full `file_manifest` table scan) and `dirRepo.LoadAll` on every fsnotify batch, and CheckScopedCaseAliases walks every baseline name and its ancestors, undoing the 'scoped cost scales with the batch' design noted a few lines above.
findings.failure_scenario: A 500k-file tree: every single-file save now loads 500k paths from SQLite and does ~500k×depth map lookups before reconciling one path — the hot path scales with the tree again.

findings.short_summary: Destination re-hashed up to 3× per action
findings.summary: checkObserved hashes the full destination content on every call, and copyBetween calls it up to three times per overwrite (claim, after preserve, after publish); deletes also now fully read each target, and the EXDEV trash path hashes 3–4×.
findings.failure_scenario: Overwriting a 2 GB file on the NAS reads it 3 times over SMB (~80 s at 76 MB/s) before the new copy lands; a remote mirror deletion of 1000 large files reads every one of them in full just to delete it. Hashing once after claim plus a cheap identity/size/mtime re-check would cover most of this.

findings.short_summary: Per-op holding dir + FS capability probe
findings.summary: claimEntry makes a holding directory and runs checkExclusivePublish (create, exclusive rename, two unlinks) for every single overwrite/delete, then renames in and out and removes the dir — roughly 8 metadata round trips per file where one unlink used to do.
findings.failure_scenario: A mirror run deleting 10k files on the SMB share does ~80k metadata round trips instead of ~10k. Probe the capability once per Tree (cache the result) and skip the probe on later claims.

findings.short_summary: Every Tree op re-walks path from root
findings.summary: Tree.directory/parent re-opens every path component from the root with openat for each Stat/Open/ReadDir/hash call, so each per-file operation costs O(depth) opens.
findings.failure_scenario: Over SMB, hashing a file 8 levels deep in ScanPaths/HashIfChanged costs ~9 network opens instead of 1; a full scan does depth-many opens per directory. Cache the directory fds during the walk or pass the parent fd down.

findings.short_summary: Inode identity check may fail on SMB
findings.summary: SameEntry compares dev/ino before vs after renaming the entry into the holding dir (RemoveFrom and checkObserved); on SMB mounts without stable server inode numbers, ino can change across rename.
findings.failure_scenario: On a cifs `noserverino` mount, or smbfs against a server without file-ID support, a rename into `.syncd-hold-*` yields a new ino → 'entry changed before removal' / ErrDestinationChanged on every remote delete and overwrite, deferred forever.

findings.short_summary: CheckCaseAliases runs twice per fast sync
findings.summary: runFastOnce calls CheckCaseAliases with the job-state baseline after ScanTrees (scanner.go:156) or scanPairForOpts (sync_once.go:456) has already run it on the same scans with a nil manifest.
findings.failure_scenario: Each fast sync folds and sorts every path in both trees twice. Pass the baseline into the scan-time check, or drop the scan-time one for the fast path.

input.recap: Reviewed PR 7 at high effort and found 10 issues. The most serious: a case-only rename can stop sync for good, and leftover holding folders can make other machines' scans fail. Findings are unverified and nothing was changed.
input.ask: Fix the top findings on this branch?

content.text:
I reviewed [william-coronado/syncd#7](https://github.com/william-coronado/syncd/pull/7) and found 10 issues. These findings haven't been checked a second time, and none of them has been tested against the real NAS.

**Correctness, in order of severity:**

1. **A case-only rename can stop sync for good.** If you rename `Report.pdf` to `report.pdf`, or delete one and create the other, the case check sees a collision on every cycle. The manifest never gets updated, so it never clears. Renaming the remote copy doesn't fix it either. The only ways out are undoing the rename or deleting the manifest database.
2. **Holding folders on the shared remote break other machines' scans.** The new `.syncd-hold-*` folders are created inside the synced tree. The scanner fails on them before it applies the ignore rules. So if another machine scans the share while this one is mid-overwrite, its whole cycle fails. A holding folder left behind by a failed check after the new file is published stops every machine until someone deletes it by hand.
3. **Remote overwrites and deletes depend on an SMB feature that may be missing.** Every overwrite, every delete (remote deletes used to be a plain unlink) and every exclusive publish now needs no-replace renames or hard links on the destination. If the Synology mount supports neither, all of these fail.
4. **File timestamps are now set before the data is flushed.** The old code deliberately set the modified time after closing the file. On SMB or NFS, the flush can overwrite it with the current time. The fast `sync` would then re-copy the file every run, and `watch` would re-hash it every cycle.
5. **The inode check may fail on SMB.** Deletes and overwrites check that the file's inode number is unchanged after moving it into the holding folder. Some SMB mounts don't keep inode numbers stable across a rename, so these would be deferred every cycle.

**Performance and cleanup:**

6. Each `watch` change batch now loads every path in the manifest, which goes against the design of keeping that cost proportional to the batch.
7. An overwrite reads the destination file up to three times to hash it, and deletes now read every file in full first.
8. Every overwrite or delete creates a holding folder and re-tests what the filesystem supports. That's about 8 network round trips per file where one unlink used to do.
9. Each file operation re-opens every folder from the sync root down to the file.
10. The fast `sync` runs the case check twice on the same scan results.

input.new_string:
`.syncd-hold-...` directories are never reconciled. One that exists only
briefly is another syncd's operation in flight on a shared remote. One that
persists (after a crash or a concurrent recreation) holds a retained
original: every scan reports it as a scan issue in the log. Inspect and
recover the retained file, then remove the holding directory. If the share
supports neither exclusive rename nor hard links, publication falls back to
check-then-rename, so a name created by another writer in that brief window
can still be replaced.

Names that differ only by case, including directory components, stop the
cycle before any transfers or deletions. This applies on all filesystems so
pairs remain safe on case-insensitive APFS and SMB destinations. One case is
handled: `watch` (and `sync --hash`) propagate a case-only rename of a
tracked, unchanged file made on one side. On a case-insensitive destination
this can take two cycles. Otherwise, resolve the reported names by giving
them distinct names, or the same spelling on both sides, before retrying.
A directory case rename needs the same rename made on the other side.

findings.short_summary: Case-only rename permanently wedges sync
findings.summary: CheckCaseAliases folds manifest/baseline paths together with both scans, so a case-only rename (or deleting `Foo` and creating `foo`) is refused before planning, and because the manifest is never updated the refusal repeats forever.
findings.failure_scenario: User renames `Report.pdf` → `report.pdf` locally. Manifest holds `Report.pdf`, local scan has `report.pdf`, remote still has `Report.pdf` → `case-insensitive path collision` on every cycle; the only escape is reverting the rename or deleting the manifest DB.

findings.short_summary: Holding dirs abort other clients' scans
findings.summary: Transient `.syncd-hold-*` directories are created inside the synced tree (including on the shared remote), and the scanner hard-fails on them before the ignore matcher runs, so any concurrent scan by another machine — or any leftover from a failed post-publish check — aborts the whole cycle.
findings.failure_scenario: Machine B's remote poll walks the share while machine A is mid-overwrite → `unfinished sync operation` → whole RunRobustOnce fails; a leftover holding dir stalls every client until manual cleanup.

findings.short_summary: Overwrites/deletes need RENAME_EXCL or hard links
findings.summary: Every robust overwrite, every delete (including network deletes that used to be a plain unlink), and every exclusive publish now requires the destination FS to support RENAME_EXCL/RENAME_NOREPLACE or hard links; on mounts with neither, all such operations fail.
findings.failure_scenario: On an SMB mount without exclusive rename or hard links, checkExclusivePublish fails → remote deletes, overwrites and new uploads all stop.

findings.short_summary: mtime now set before fsync/close
findings.summary: The preserved mtime is applied before `tmp.Sync()`/`tmp.Close()`, whereas the old code deliberately set it after closing; on network filesystems, cached writes flushed at fsync/close can bump the mtime to 'now'.
findings.failure_scenario: Download/upload to smbfs or NFS: buffered data flushed after utimes resets last-write time, so fast sync re-copies forever and robust HashIfChanged re-hashes every cycle.

findings.short_summary: Scoped cycle loads full manifest names per batch
findings.summary: RunRobustScoped now calls `Repo.LoadNames` (a full `file_manifest` table scan) and `dirRepo.LoadAll` on every fsnotify batch, and CheckScopedCaseAliases walks every baseline name and its ancestors.
findings.failure_scenario: A 500k-file tree: every single-file save loads 500k paths from SQLite before reconciling one path.

findings.short_summary: Destination re-hashed up to 3× per action
findings.summary: checkObserved hashes the full destination content on every call, and copyBetween calls it up to three times per overwrite; deletes also fully read each target, and the EXDEV trash path hashes 3–4×.
findings.failure_scenario: Overwriting a 2 GB file on the NAS reads it 3 times over SMB before the new copy lands.

findings.short_summary: Per-op holding dir + FS capability probe
findings.summary: claimEntry makes a holding directory and runs checkExclusivePublish for every single overwrite/delete — roughly 8 metadata round trips per file where one unlink used to do.
findings.failure_scenario: A mirror run deleting 10k files on the SMB share does ~80k metadata round trips instead of ~10k.

findings.summary: Tree.directory/parent re-opens every path component from the root with openat for each Stat/Open/ReadDir/hash call.

content.text:
I fixed the top 4 findings on `codex/fix-sync-safety`. Build, vet, the full test suite, `-race` and both cross-builds pass on this Mac. Nothing is committed yet.

1. **A case-only rename no longer stops sync for good** ([aliases.go](internal/fs/aliases.go)).
   - Only names that actually exist on a side are compared now. A manifest spelling that's gone from both sides no longer blocks the pair, so renaming both sides the same way clears a collision.
   - One case now goes through: a file renamed by case on one side, where the other side still has the old spelling with unchanged content (checked by hash). The planner turns it into a delete of the old name and a create of the new one. On a case-insensitive destination this can take two cycles.
   - The fast `sync` keeps no hashes, so it never gets this exception and stays strict as before.
   - In `watch`, the per-batch check can't tell a rename from a real collision, so when it trips it now runs a full cycle ([sync_loop.go](internal/app/sync_loop.go)). The full cycle either passes the rename on or refuses with the same error.
   - Real collisions are still refused: two spellings on one side, a folder renamed by case, or a renamed file whose old copy was edited.
2. **Holding folders no longer abort scans** ([scanner.go](internal/fs/scanner.go)). The scanner skips them and logs a warning every scan, so a kept original isn't forgotten. The per-batch case check in `watch` now skips them too.
3. **Mounts without no-replace renames or hard links now work** ([claim.go](internal/fs/claim.go)). When neither is available, syncd checks that the destination name is free and then does a plain rename. This is no worse than before the PR: another writer creating that name in that short gap can still be overwritten. I also removed the per-operation probe that tested for these features.
4. **The file's modified time is set after the data is flushed and the file closed** ([atomic_copy.go](internal/fs/atomic_copy.go)), as the old code did.

**Tests:** I added tests for the rename exception and its refusals, the `watch` rename going through, a real collision still refused, a scan skipping a holding folder, and writes and deletes on a mount without either feature. Two existing tests pinned the old behavior, so I rewrote them: one expected a scan to stop on a holding folder, the other expected a case-only rename to be refused. I also updated the "Filesystem safety" section of the README.

**Not tested:**
- The two-cycle rename test ran on this Mac's disk; Linux, where names are case-sensitive, wasn't tested.
- Neither the new fallback nor the timestamp order has been tried on the actual Synology share. The fallback is only tested by faking the missing features.

The other six findings, all performance or cleanup apart from the inode check on SMB, are left as they were.
Commit the working tree changes with a sensible message.
